blocks.text:
Design a Car Rental System that lets customers reserve a vehicle at one branch, pick it up, drive it, and return it at any branch in the network (a one-way rental). The system must track vehicle availability in real time, price rentals by vehicle category and duration, charge a fee when a vehicle is dropped off at a different branch than it was picked up from, and charge a late fee when a vehicle is returned after its planned rental period ends.

  • Actors: Customer (reserves, picks up, returns a vehicle), Branch Staff (implicitly, via the system marking vehicle status), CarRentalService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: single rental company with multiple branches, vehicle categories with per-day pricing, one-way transfers, late-return fees.

This is a smaller cousin of the Hotel Management System: instead of a date-range calendar per room, a vehicle simply has one active reservation at a time, but adds cross-branch transfer billing that hotel-management-system does not need.
The system must support the following core capabilities for customers and the rental operator:

items: Vehicle inventory: register vehicles at branches, grouped by category (ECONOMY, SUV, LUXURY).
Reservation: a customer requests a vehicle category, a pickup branch, a dropoff branch, and a number of planned days.
Pickup: once at the pickup branch, the customer collects the reserved vehicle and the rental clock starts.
Return: the customer drops the vehicle off (possibly at a different branch) and a bill is generated.
Billing: base cost by category and duration, a one-way fee if pickup and dropoff branches differ, and a late fee if the vehicle is returned after the planned duration.
Rejection: if no vehicle of the requested category is available at the pickup branch, the reservation is rejected with a clear reason.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: adding new branches or vehicles must not require touching existing reservation logic.
Extensibility: new pricing tiers (weekend rates, loyalty discounts) or vehicle categories should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: pricing, notification, and vehicle-creation concerns are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: vehicle lookup and availability checks are O(1) via an in-memory map.
Thread safety: two customers reserving the same last available vehicle concurrently must not both succeed.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Can a customer reserve a specific vehicle, or only a category (with any matching vehicle assigned at pickup)?
Is a reservation locked to a specific date range in advance, or is it always "starting now" (walk-in style)?
Should we support cancellations before pickup?
Is there a fixed one-way fee, or does it vary by distance between branches?
Should damage/fuel charges be modeled, or is billing limited to time and location fees?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: A reservation is category-based (ECONOMY/SUV/LUXURY), not a specific vehicle id, and is created at "now" rather than against a future date-range calendar. Advance date-range booking with overlap checking is deliberately out of scope here since that exact mechanic is already covered in depth by the Hotel Management System design; this problem instead focuses on cross-branch transfer and time-based billing.
Each vehicle can be involved in at most one active reservation at a time (RESERVED or RENTED); it becomes AVAILABLE again only after return.
The one-way fee is a flat fee (for simplicity) charged whenever pickup and dropoff branches differ, rather than a distance-computed fee.
The late fee is charged at 1.5x the daily rate for every day beyond the planned duration.
Cancellations, damage assessment, and fuel-level charges are noted as future extensions, not implemented.

blocks.text: The design centers on six core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: Branch, Vehicle, VehicleCategory, Customer, Reservation, Bill

items: Branch: a physical location that stocks vehicles.
Vehicle: a rentable unit with a category and a status (AVAILABLE, RESERVED, RENTED).
VehicleCategory: an enum (ECONOMY, SUV, LUXURY) driving the daily rate.
Customer: the person renting the vehicle.
Reservation: a request tying a customer to a vehicle, a pickup branch, a dropoff branch, and a planned duration.
Bill: the computed charge for a completed rental.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A branch has many vehicles; a customer makes many reservations; a reservation references exactly one vehicle and produces one bill

items: Branch to Vehicle is one-to-many (composition-like: vehicles belong to whichever branch currently holds them).
Customer to Reservation is one-to-many.
Reservation to Vehicle is many-to-one (many reservations over time reference the same vehicle, never concurrently).
Reservation to Bill is one-to-one, created at return time.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep pricing, notification, and vehicle creation decoupled from the core service.
Why needed: the daily rate depends on vehicle category, and duration-based discounts may change independently of the rest of the system.

Why it is the best fit: a new pricing scheme (e.g., weekend surcharge) can be added as a new class implementing the same interface, with zero changes to CarRentalService. What it solves: it isolates a business rule that changes often (pricing) from a component that should stay stable (the orchestration logic).
Why needed: reservation confirmations, rejections, pickups, and returns are all events other parts of a real system (email, SMS, analytics) would want to react to.

metadata.alt: RentalObserver interface notified by CarRentalService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: CarRentalService does not need to know who is listening or why. What it solves: it decouples the core rental workflow from side effects.
Why needed: vehicle id generation and category-based defaults should not be scattered across setup code.

Why it is the best fit: onboarding a new branch with a batch of vehicles becomes a single factory call. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide across branches.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Branch: attributes branchId, city; responsibility: identify a physical location.
Vehicle: attributes vehicleId, category, currentBranchId, status; responsibility: track where a vehicle is and whether it can be rented.
VehicleFactory: method createVehicles(branch, category, count); responsibility: generate correctly-prefixed vehicle ids.
Reservation: attributes reservationId, customerId, vehicleId, pickupBranchId, dropoffBranchId, plannedDays, status; responsibility: capture a single rental request end-to-end.
Bill: attributes baseCost, oneWayFee, lateFee; method getTotal(); responsibility: represent a finalized charge.
CarRentalService: the orchestrator; responsibility: find an available vehicle, create reservations, process pickup and return, compute bills, and notify observers.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: VehiclePricingStrategy and RentalObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: VehiclePricingStrategy: calculateCost(vehicle, days, pickupBranch, dropoffBranch): abstracts away exactly how a price is derived.
RentalObserver: onReservationConfirmed / onReservationRejected / onVehiclePickedUp / onVehicleReturned: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: Three flows below cover the successful one-way rental, a rejection due to unavailability, and a late return.

metadata.alt: Alice reserves ECO1 at BR1, drops it off at BR2, and pays a one-way fee
Bob tries to reserve an ECONOMY vehicle at BR1 while ECO1 is already rented
Carol returns SUV1 a day later than planned and is charged a late fee

blocks.text: The end-to-end happy path, alongside its failure branch, looks like this:

metadata.alt: Reserve, check availability, pick up, drive, return, bill

items: Happy path: reserve → vehicle found → mark RESERVED → pick up → mark RENTED → return → compute bill → mark AVAILABLE at dropoff branch.
Failure path: reserve → no matching vehicle at pickup branch → reject with reason, no state change.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: reserveVehicle(customerId, category, pickupBranchId, dropoffBranchId, plannedDays): finds an available vehicle of the requested category at the pickup branch and creates a reservation, or throws if none is free.
pickUp(reservationId): transitions the vehicle to RENTED and records the pickup moment.
returnVehicle(reservationId, actualDays): computes and returns the Bill, and frees the vehicle at the dropoff branch.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: VehicleNotAvailableException: no vehicle of the requested category is free at the pickup branch.
InvalidReservationException: an unknown reservation id, customer id, or a non-positive planned duration.
VehicleNotRentedException: returnVehicle is called on a reservation whose vehicle was never picked up.

blocks.text: The critical race is two customers reserving the last available vehicle of a category at the same branch simultaneously.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to reserve the same vehicle; synchronization ensures only one wins

blocks.text: Synchronizing the availability-check-and-mark step (per vehicle, or per branch-category bucket) ensures the check and the status update happen atomically, so only one reservation can ever claim a given vehicle.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new pricing scheme (weekend surcharge, loyalty discount) is a new VehiclePricingStrategy implementation, swapped in without touching CarRentalService.
A new notification channel (SMS, push) is a new RentalObserver implementation.
A new vehicle category is a new enum value plus a rate entry, not a structural change.
Distance-based one-way fees can replace the flat fee inside the pricing strategy alone.
Single Responsibility: Vehicle tracks state, VehiclePricingStrategy computes cost, RentalObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new pricing or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to CarRentalService.
Liskov Substitution: any VehiclePricingStrategy or RentalObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: RentalObserver exposes only the four lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: CarRentalService depends on the VehiclePricingStrategy and RentalObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
Customer returns the vehicle at the same branch it was picked up from, so no one-way fee applies.
Customer returns exactly on the planned day, so no late fee applies.
Requested category has vehicles at other branches but none free at the requested pickup branch, so the reservation is still rejected (no cross-branch auto-transfer).
returnVehicle called twice for the same reservation: the second call throws VehicleNotRentedException.
reserveVehicle: O(V) to scan vehicles at a branch for a free match in category, where V is vehicles at that branch (or O(1) with a per-branch-category free-list).
pickUp / returnVehicle: O(1) map lookups by reservationId and vehicleId.
Space: O(V + R) for V vehicles and R reservations held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: Branch, Vehicle, Customer, Reservation, Bill

items: An index on Vehicle(currentBranchId, category, status) speeds up the "find a free vehicle at this branch" query.
Bill is a one-to-one child of Reservation, created only at return time.
Support advance date-range reservations with overlap checking (as in Hotel Management System) instead of walk-in-only bookings.
Replace the flat one-way fee with a real distance/route-based calculation between branches.
Add cancellation and no-show handling.
Add damage assessment and fuel-level charges at return time.
In a distributed deployment, move vehicle-status locking to a database-level row lock or a distributed lock rather than in-process synchronization.

from enum import Enum

# Vehicle category drives the daily rental rate.
class VehicleCategory(Enum):
    ECONOMY = "ECONOMY"  # cheapest tier
    SUV = "SUV"          # mid tier
    LUXURY = "LUXURY"    # premium tier

# Lifecycle status of a single vehicle.
class VehicleStatus(Enum):
    AVAILABLE = "AVAILABLE"  # free to be reserved
    RESERVED = "RESERVED"    # claimed but not yet picked up
    RENTED = "RENTED"        # currently with a customer

# A single rentable vehicle.
class Vehicle:
    def __init__(self, vehicle_id, category, branch_id):
        self.vehicle_id = vehicle_id        # unique id, e.g. ECO1
        self.category = category            # pricing tier
        self.current_branch_id = branch_id  # branch that currently holds it
        self.status = VehicleStatus.AVAILABLE  # new vehicles start free

    def is_available(self):
        return self.status == VehicleStatus.AVAILABLE  # convenience check

# Creates vehicles with category-prefixed ids for a branch.
class VehicleFactory:
    def __init__(self):
        self.counters = {}  # prefix -> how many already created

    def create_vehicles(self, branch_id, category, count):
        prefix = self._prefix_for(category)  # e.g. "ECO"
        created = []                          # result list
        for _ in range(count):                # create 'count' vehicles
            n = self.counters.get(prefix, 0) + 1  # next number for this prefix
            self.counters[prefix] = n              # remember it
            created.append(Vehicle(f"{prefix}{n}", category, branch_id))  # e.g. ECO1
        return created  # hand back the new vehicles

    def _prefix_for(self, category):
        if category == VehicleCategory.ECONOMY:  # economy prefix
            return "ECO"
        if category == VehicleCategory.SUV:       # suv prefix
            return "SUV"
        return "LUX"                               # luxury prefix

# Strategy interface: how a rental's cost is computed.
class VehiclePricingStrategy:
    def calculate_cost(self, vehicle, days, pickup_branch_id, dropoff_branch_id):
        raise NotImplementedError  # concrete strategies must implement this

# Standard pricing: per-category daily rate, discount for long rentals.
class StandardVehiclePricingStrategy(VehiclePricingStrategy):
    def _daily_rate(self, category):
        if category == VehicleCategory.ECONOMY:  # economy rate
            return 40.0
        if category == VehicleCategory.SUV:       # suv rate
            return 70.0
        return 120.0                               # luxury rate

    def calculate_cost(self, vehicle, days, pickup_branch_id, dropoff_branch_id):
        rate = self._daily_rate(vehicle.category)  # base per-day rate
        base = rate * days                          # total before discount
        if days >= 7:                                # long-duration discount
            base = base * 0.9                         # 10 percent off
        return base  # final base cost (fees added separately)

# A single rental request end-to-end.
class Reservation:
    def __init__(self, reservation_id, customer_id, vehicle_id,
                 pickup_branch_id, dropoff_branch_id, planned_days):
        self.reservation_id = reservation_id      # unique id
        self.customer_id = customer_id            # who booked it
        self.vehicle_id = vehicle_id              # which vehicle
        self.pickup_branch_id = pickup_branch_id  # where it starts
        self.dropoff_branch_id = dropoff_branch_id  # where it ends
        self.planned_days = planned_days          # how long it was planned for
        self.status = "CONFIRMED"                 # starts confirmed

# The final computed charge for a completed rental.
class Bill:
    def __init__(self, base_cost, one_way_fee, late_fee):
        self.base_cost = base_cost    # rate times days (minus discount)
        self.one_way_fee = one_way_fee  # charged if pickup != dropoff branch
        self.late_fee = late_fee      # charged if returned late

    def get_total(self):
        return self.base_cost + self.one_way_fee + self.late_fee  # sum of all charges

# Observer interface: reacts to rental lifecycle events.
class RentalObserver:
    def on_reservation_confirmed(self, reservation): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_reservation_rejected(self, customer_id, reason): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_vehicle_picked_up(self, reservation): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_vehicle_returned(self, reservation, bill): raise NotImplementedError

# Simple observer that prints events to the console.
class ConsoleRentalObserver(RentalObserver):
    def on_reservation_confirmed(self, reservation):
        print(f"Reservation {reservation.reservation_id} confirmed for customer {reservation.customer_id}")

    def on_reservation_rejected(self, customer_id, reason):
        print(f"Reservation rejected for customer {customer_id}: {reason}")

    def on_vehicle_picked_up(self, reservation):
        print(f"Vehicle {reservation.vehicle_id} picked up by {reservation.customer_id}")

    def on_vehicle_returned(self, reservation, bill):
        print(f"Vehicle {reservation.vehicle_id} returned by {reservation.customer_id}, total: {bill.get_total()}")

# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class VehicleNotAvailableException(Exception): pass
class InvalidReservationException(Exception): pass
class VehicleNotRentedException(Exception): pass

# The core orchestrator tying every piece together.
class CarRentalService:
    def __init__(self, pricing_strategy):
        self.vehicles = {}       # vehicleId -> Vehicle
        self.reservations = {}   # reservationId -> Reservation
        self.pricing_strategy = pricing_strategy  # pluggable pricing
        self.observers = []       # listeners
        self.reservation_counter = 0  # simple id generator

    def add_vehicle(self, vehicle):
        self.vehicles[vehicle.vehicle_id] = vehicle  # register a vehicle

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def reserve_vehicle(self, customer_id, category, pickup_branch_id, dropoff_branch_id, planned_days):
        if planned_days <= 0:  # guard against bad input
            raise InvalidReservationException("planned_days must be positive")
        found = None  # will hold the matching vehicle
        for v in self.vehicles.values():  # scan all vehicles
            if v.category == category and v.current_branch_id == pickup_branch_id and v.is_available():
                found = v  # remember it
                break       # stop at first match
        if found is None:  # nothing matched
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_reservation_rejected(customer_id, "Vehicle not available")  # notify
            raise VehicleNotAvailableException(f"No {category} vehicle available at {pickup_branch_id}")
        found.status = VehicleStatus.RESERVED  # claim the vehicle
        self.reservation_counter += 1            # bump id counter
        reservation_id = f"RES-{self.reservation_counter}"  # build id
        reservation = Reservation(reservation_id, customer_id, found.vehicle_id,
                                   pickup_branch_id, dropoff_branch_id, planned_days)  # build reservation
        self.reservations[reservation_id] = reservation  # store it
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_reservation_confirmed(reservation)  # notify
        return reservation  # hand back to caller

    def pick_up(self, reservation_id):
        reservation = self.reservations.get(reservation_id)  # look up reservation
        if reservation is None:
            raise InvalidReservationException(f"Unknown reservation: {reservation_id}")
        vehicle = self.vehicles[reservation.vehicle_id]  # look up vehicle
        vehicle.status = VehicleStatus.RENTED             # mark rented
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_vehicle_picked_up(reservation)  # notify

    def return_vehicle(self, reservation_id, actual_days):
        reservation = self.reservations.get(reservation_id)  # look up reservation
        if reservation is None:
            raise InvalidReservationException(f"Unknown reservation: {reservation_id}")
        vehicle = self.vehicles[reservation.vehicle_id]  # look up vehicle
        if vehicle.status != VehicleStatus.RENTED:  # must currently be rented
            raise VehicleNotRentedException(f"Vehicle {vehicle.vehicle_id} is not currently rented")
        base = self.pricing_strategy.calculate_cost(vehicle, reservation.planned_days,
                                                      reservation.pickup_branch_id, reservation.dropoff_branch_id)  # base cost
        one_way_fee = 0.0 if reservation.pickup_branch_id == reservation.dropoff_branch_id else 25.0  # flat fee if branches differ
        late_days = max(0, actual_days-reservation.planned_days)  # days beyond plan
        daily_rate = base / max(1, reservation.planned_days)       # approximate per-day rate for late fee
        late_fee = late_days * daily_rate * 1.5                     # 1.5x rate per late day
        bill = Bill(base, one_way_fee, late_fee)                     # build bill
        vehicle.status = VehicleStatus.AVAILABLE                     # free the vehicle
        vehicle.current_branch_id = reservation.dropoff_branch_id    # it now lives at the dropoff branch
        reservation.status = "RETURNED"                              # mark reservation done
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_vehicle_returned(reservation, bill)  # notify
        return bill  # hand back to caller

items: Why is pricing a Strategy rather than a switch statement inside the service? Because pricing rules change independently and often carry business-specific tweaks (promotions, loyalty tiers) that should not risk breaking the reservation workflow.

Why does the vehicle track its own currentBranchId rather than the service maintaining a per-branch vehicle list? Simpler invariant: the vehicle is always the single source of truth for where it physically is.
How would you support reserving a specific vehicle instead of just a category? Add an overloaded reserveVehicle(customerId, vehicleId, ...) that skips the scan and directly checks that one vehicle.
Flat one-way fee vs distance-based fee: flat fee is simpler to reason about and test, at the cost of not reflecting real transfer cost; a production system would price this per branch pair.

Category-based reservation vs specific-vehicle reservation: category-based is simpler and mirrors how most real rental counters actually operate (you reserve a class of car, not a VIN), but sacrifices the ability to guarantee a particular vehicle in advance.

In-memory synchronized lock vs database transaction: in-memory is fine for a single-process demo; a distributed deployment would need a database-level unique constraint or distributed lock on vehicle assignment.
Persist vehicles, reservations, and bills in a relational database rather than in-memory maps, using the schema in the Database Design section.
Emit reservation/pickup/return events to a message queue so downstream systems (billing, analytics, notifications) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Add idempotency keys to reserveVehicle so retried network requests cannot create duplicate reservations.
Expose metrics on vehicle utilization per branch and category to guide fleet rebalancing.
